title: Fit a spin-on oil filter: gasket contact, then three quarters to one turn by hand, not left loose or cranked on
context: Changing the oil and filter is one of the most familiar pieces of car and motorcycle upkeep: most drivers have it done every few months, and many do it themselves at home. Filter makers print it on the can: spin the filter on until its gasket contacts the base, then tighten it a further three quarters of a turn by hand (some say three quarters to one turn). A filter left at contact or a little past it can work loose under engine vibration and leak oil, while one cranked on well past a full turn can crush its gasket, which can roll out of its groove and blow out under oil pressure, and may not come off by hand at the next change. Here a new filter has been started on the thread of a filter head bolted to the bench and stops three quarters of a turn short of gasket contact.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A die-cast aluminum remote oil filter mount (filter head) is bolted to the bench with four bolts: a block 7.5 cm deep (x), 9 cm wide (y) and 3.4 cm tall, with a round machined gasket land 7.2 cm across and 0.6 cm tall on top, so the gasket face is at z 4. Its threaded M20 x 1.5 nipple points straight up at x 30, y -12. Its two hose ports, on its left and right sides, are closed with gray plastic plugs, and a black witness line is painted on the front of the land and block. A new spin-on oil filter, 250 g, is threaded onto the nipple: a black painted steel can 6.6 cm across and 7 cm tall with a plain flat top, grip flutes around its top edge, a white printed band, a black rubber gasket on its base, a printed index stripe down its side (white on the black, black across the band), and three black quarter-turn ticks on the band. The thread is right-handed (tightens clockwise seen from above) and advances 1.5 mm per turn. The filter starts about four turns onto the nipple (five at gasket contact) and three quarters of a turn (270 degrees) short of gasket contact, its gasket 1.1 mm above the land on the real thread (about 0.3 mm in the sim, as the fidelity notes) and its index stripe facing left; at gasket contact the stripe faces the robot, lined up with the witness line. Nothing else is on the bench.
scoring: The filter's angle is measured from gasket contact over the whole run, positive when tightened past it (it starts at -270 degrees). Doing nothing scores 0. Two events score 0 for good. The filter coming off its thread at any point (unscrewed 4.25 turns from its start, five back from contact) undoes the fit, and starting it again risks cross-threading it. The filter ever tightened more than 450 degrees (1.25 turns) past contact over-compresses the gasket, which can roll out of its groove, and backing off does not restore it; the sim does not deform the gasket, so the angle is the proxy, and a real trial checks the gasket for a flattened or rolled lip after the trial. At the end the score is 0 if the filter is under 90 degrees past contact, a third of the least any maker asks, loose enough to work loose under vibration. It is also 0 if more than 45 degrees of the new ground gained past contact was not turned by a holding hand's own wrist, since the makers' rule is to tighten by hand, and a swipe or knock overshoots or stops short without control. A hand holds the filter when its fingers are closed on the can (opening from 15 % of full travel tighter to 3 % looser than the can's width) with the tool point within 1.5 cm of the can's axis, anywhere from 1 cm above the gasket face to 1.5 cm above the top. Each step, a holding hand credits only as much turning as its wrist rolled clockwise (at most 30 degrees carried ahead of the filter). A second hand near the can, or on it helping, does not void a holding hand's turning; with both on it, the larger wrist roll counts. Turning back and forth over the same angles counts once. The 45 degrees cover the filter settling as the hand lets go; a real trial checks the video for a swipe. Otherwise: 0.25 for 90 to 180 degrees, past contact and sealing but at most two thirds of the makers' figure, so it can still loosen. 0.5 for 180 to 240 degrees, close to the figure but short of it, or for 360 to 450 degrees or ever past 360, past the most any maker allows and hard to remove by hand but not crushed. 1.0 for 240 to 360 degrees and never past 360: the makers' three quarters to one turn, less 30 degrees for judging it by hand against the can's quarter-turn ticks. Any score is capped at 0.5 while a hand is still on the filter at the end, because the fit is not finished while a hand can still turn it either way. A hand is on it when it holds the can as above, or when its palm or fingers touch the can: the gripper's own shape (boxes fitted to the YAM's collision meshes, at the fingers' present opening) within 2 mm of it, the solver's resting gap. A hand hovering beside or over the can, open or closed, is not on it. A real trial checks the last frames for a pad or finger on the can. Where the arms end is not scored. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. In a real trial the turn is read from witness marks: before the trial, spin the filter to gasket contact, draw a line across the can and the head, back it off three quarters of a turn, and tape a protractor ring with 15-degree marks around the land. Afterwards read the can's line against the ring, count whole turns from the video and photograph it from above.
reset_notes: Unscrew the filter, wipe and re-oil its gasket, spin it back on to gasket contact, check the witness lines meet, and back it off three quarters of a turn. Replace the filter if it was tightened past a full turn (its gasket is deformed).
fidelity: True size; the filter points up so a straight-down grip reaches it (some remote mounts carry it so). The thread is modeled: a slide coupled to a hinge, 1.5 mm per turn. The slide's spring sags 0.8 mm under the filter, so the gasket starts 0.3 mm up. Past contact a turning friction grows 0.1 N·m per radian (capped at 1 N·m), against about 15 to 20 N·m by hand in reality. No oil, gasket deformation or leak is simulated; a real trial reads the turn from witness marks.
